messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Certain Songs: Certain songs, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martin Weiss is a 56-year-old married American dancer who came to treatment months after an accident in which another person was seriously injured, an event he speaks about with a mixture of shame and stunned disbelief. The injury happened on an ordinary day that had begun with rehearsals and errands, and he still remembers the abruptness with which it split his life into a before and an after. He had been driving when a collision occurred, and although he was not physically the one most gravely hurt, he experienced the event as something he had failed to prevent. What remains most vivid to him is not a neat sequence but the sight of the other car after impact, bent and struck in a way that still feels unbearable to picture. In session, when he edges close to describing it, he stops, looks away, and says that what he sees is “that car, hit like that,” as if the image is less a memory than a scene that forces itself in front of him.

In the first weeks afterward, Martin expected to feel shaken, but he was unprepared for how often pieces of the event would break into daily life. If he passed a roadway accident, even from a distance, his body tightened before he had fully registered what he was seeing. Images of cars hit at odd angles could seize his attention and leave him momentarily elsewhere. Certain songs became unexpectedly loaded. A song playing in a store, in the car, or from a speaker in the studio could stop him cold if it matched the music that had been around the time of the accident or had become linked in his mind with that day. He found himself leaving spaces abruptly, unable to explain to others why a familiar melody had suddenly made him feel cornered.

Martin’s work as a dancer made this especially difficult. Rehearsal spaces that once felt sustaining now often felt overstimulating, especially when they were crowded. In a full studio, with music on, bodies moving close around him, and too much happening at once, he became acutely uncomfortable and restless. He could not settle into combinations the way he once had. He would lose the thread of choreography, miss counts, or find his attention pulled away by the press of people and sound. He had begun to think of himself as someone who could no longer rely on his own mind. Even when he knew he was physically safe, his body did not seem to agree; he remained keyed up, scanning, unable to relax.

At home, the nights were often the hardest. Martin told his wife that sleep felt impossible unless he stayed alert, as though letting down his guard would be irresponsible. He delayed going to bed, lay awake listening, and resisted the moment of drifting off. During the day he tried forcefully not to think about the accident, cutting off thoughts the instant they appeared. He also began avoiding the location where it happened, changing routes and refusing suggestions that would take him nearby. These decisions made immediate sense to him. He believed that if he let himself think too much, or if he went back there, he would be overwhelmed by what he had failed to stop.

Over time, his mind returned repeatedly to the person he believed he had been before the accident. He dwelled on his former ease, his confidence, his ability to move through crowded environments and focus completely on music and performance. He compared that version of himself to the man he now experienced as tense, distracted, and morally diminished. What weighed heaviest was not only that someone else had been seriously injured, but his conviction that he had not done enough. He says, with a fixed certainty, that he will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. He has come to see the event through the language of failure: he should have protected others, and he failed; he failed in what he considers his most important role in life. He does not talk about this abstractly. He means husband, adult, responsible person, someone who should have kept other people safe.

By the time he sought help, these patterns had narrowed his life. Rehearsals felt harder to get through, crowded settings increasingly intolerable, and his wife had begun to notice how often he withdrew, rerouted plans, or went silent when certain songs came on. He came to treatment not because he doubts the seriousness of what happened, but because he is exhausted by living in constant readiness and by the feeling that the world can tilt back into that moment without warning. What frightens him most is that this is now who he is: a man defined by one failure, unable to protect, unable to rest. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase the event, but to be able to hear music, enter a crowded room, and lie down at night without feeling he has to keep watch forever.
